about: Curated by SkillSim for practice. These notes describe common usage in many US/English-speaking offices; they are not universal, not externally verified, and norms vary by organization, industry, region, and culture.

general.norms_vary: Directness, formality, and how disagreement is expressed differ across workplaces and cultures. A softer or more direct style is not automatically better; what matters is that the message is understood and the relationship holds.
general.power_and_silence: People with less positional power often avoid raising problems with someone who controls their review, pay, or contract. Silence does not necessarily mean agreement or lack of concern.
general.asking_is_normal: Asking what a term means or what someone expects is common and usually seen as careful rather than uninformed.

phrases.one-on-one: A recurring private meeting between a manager and a direct report. It can be used for status updates, support, career talk, or feedback; the purpose varies by team.
phrases.sprint: A fixed work period (often 1–2 weeks) in agile teams. A 'missed sprint deadline' usually means planned work wasn't finished by the end of that period.
phrases.blocked: Someone can't continue their work until another task is done. 'Engineering is blocked' means engineers are waiting on this work.
phrases.handoff: The point where one person's finished work passes to the next person, for example designs going to engineers.
phrases.it's been a lot: Often a soft signal of overload or stress. It can invite a follow-up question; it may also be a way of avoiding details.
phrases.on my plate: The set of tasks someone is responsible for right now.
phrases.bandwidth: Informal for available time or capacity.
phrases.performance review: A formal evaluation, often tied to promotions or raises. Mentioning it can be heard as a warning, even if not intended.

dynamics: The team lead controls Jordan's priorities and has influence on their review, so Jordan may be cautious about admitting problems.
A request from a more senior person outside the team (such as a VP) can feel hard to refuse, even if it isn't in the plan.
Jordan is relatively new (eight months), which can make someone more worried about looking less capable.
uncertainties: Why the deadlines were missed is not known at the start; it could be workload, unclear requirements, personal factors, or something else.
Whether Jordan knows how much the delays affect engineering is unclear.
It's unclear whether anyone else, such as another leader, has asked Jordan for work.
questions: What's been taking up your time over the last few sprints?
Is there anything on your plate I might not know about?
What would make Thursday's handoff realistic for you?
How would you like us to flag risks earlier next time?

phrases.base: The fixed annual salary, separate from bonuses, equity, or benefits.
phrases.band: The salary range a company has approved for a role or level. Recruiters often can't go above it without extra approval.
phrases.internal equity: Keeping pay consistent among people in similar roles. It can be a real constraint or a negotiating position; often both.
phrases.signing bonus: A one-time payment for accepting an offer. Companies sometimes use it when base salary is harder to change.
phrases.verbal yes: An informal acceptance before signing the written offer. Many people consider it a commitment, so it's worth being sure of the terms first.
phrases.comp review: A scheduled review of compensation, sometimes earlier than the normal annual cycle if negotiated.
phrases.let me see what I can do: Often signals some flexibility exists, but not how much. It may also be a polite way to end the topic.
phrases.competing offer: Another company's offer or late-stage interview. Mentioning it can add leverage; overstating it can damage trust.

dynamics: The recruiter holds the offer, but the company has spent months looking, which gives the candidate some leverage.
Recruiters usually represent the company's budget and may also genuinely want the candidate to accept.
Candidates from backgrounds where negotiating is less common may feel it is rude; in many companies, a polite counteroffer is expected.
uncertainties: The exact top of the salary band is not known to the candidate.
Whether other parts of the package (bonus, review timing, start date) are flexible is not known until asked.
How firm the decision deadline is may be unclear.
questions: Is there flexibility on base salary for this role?
Beyond base, which parts of the package can be adjusted?
Could you share the range approved for this level?
When do you need a decision, and could the terms be confirmed in writing first?

phrases.go live: The moment a product or system becomes available to real users.
phrases.integration bug: An error where two systems that need to work together (here, the portal and the scheduling system) don't connect properly.
phrases.accountability: Here, usually a request for someone to clearly own what went wrong and what happens next, not necessarily a demand for blame or punishment.
phrases.in writing: A documented summary, often so the client can share it with their own leadership. It can also signal reduced trust.
phrases.escalate: To raise an issue to more senior people. A client mentioning escalation may be signaling pressure from their side.
phrases.renewal: When the client decides whether to continue the contract. Upcoming renewals raise the stakes of every interaction.
phrases.credit: A discount or refund offered to make up for a problem. Clients may or may not expect one.

dynamics: The client director is accountable to their own CEO, so part of their frustration may be about how this looks internally.
The contract renewal gives the client real leverage over the vendor.
The account manager speaks for a team whose mistake caused the delay, which can make people defensive or overly apologetic.
uncertainties: Whether the client wants compensation, reassurance, or mainly a credible plan is not clear at first.
How much detail about the technical cause the client actually wants is unknown.
Whether the new date is fully certain depends on the fix being verified.
questions: What would be most helpful for you to share with your leadership today?
How much technical detail would be useful for you?
Who on your side should be on the follow-up updates?
What would make the new date feel credible to you?
